section.title: Job Restored
section.sectionRationale: The book closes with a double reversal. First, God rebukes Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar by name for not having spoken of Him what is right, as His servant Job had, and requires them to be reconciled to God only through Job's own intercessory prayer for them. Then, after Job prays for the very friends who wounded him, the LORD restores his fortunes, doubling everything he had, surrounding him again with family, and giving him a long, full life.
section.thesis: Job's vindication comes not because his suffering is finally explained but because he is proven to have spoken rightly about God, and his restoration comes not merely as compensation for loss but as the fruit of forgiving and interceding for the very friends who had accused him falsely.
section.frameNote: Four movements: God's rebuke of the three friends and His command that they seek reconciliation only through Job's prayer; the LORD's restoration of Job's fortunes after Job prays for his friends, with family and former acquaintances gathering to comfort him; the doubling of Job's flocks and the birth of new children, including three uniquely named and honored daughters; and the closing report of Job's long, full life, dying old and satisfied with days.

units.label: God rebukes the three friends
units.note: you have not spoken of Me what is right

verses.text: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.

So now, take seven bulls and seven rams, go to My servant Job, and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. Then My servant Job will pray for you, for I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken accurately about Me, as My servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the LORD had told them; and the LORD accepted Job’s request.

units.label: The LORD restores Job's fortunes
units.note: after Job had prayed for his friends

verses.text: After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD {{shuv|restored}} his prosperity and doubled his former possessions.

All his brothers and sisters and prior acquaintances came and dined with him in his house. They consoled him and comforted him over all the adversity that the LORD had brought upon him. And each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring.

units.label: A new family, a new blessing
units.note: no women as beautiful as Job's daughters

verses.text: So the LORD blessed Job’s latter days more than his first. He owned 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys.
And he also had seven sons and three daughters.
He named his first daughter Jemimah, his second Keziah, and his third Keren-happuch.
No women as beautiful as Job’s daughters could be found in all the land, and their father granted them an {{nachalah|inheritance}} among their brothers.

units.label: Old and full of years
units.note: Job died, old and full of years

verses.text: After this, Job lived 140 years and saw his children and their children to the fourth generation.
And so Job died, old and {{saba|full}} of years.

shuv.gloss: To turn or restore a captivity or fortune, a phrase used elsewhere for national restoration, Deuteronomy 30:3, Psalm 126:1. Its use here elevates Job's personal restoration to the scale of a small exodus, God reversing complete ruin into abundant blessing.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted portion. That Job's three daughters receive an inheritance alongside their seven brothers is culturally remarkable in the ancient world, showing Job's restored household extending even greater honor and provision to his daughters than convention required.

saba.gloss: Satisfied, full, having had enough. The book's closing phrase, 'old and full of years,' uses the same word for contented satisfaction found in blessings elsewhere, Genesis 25:8, Genesis 35:29, marking Job's life as complete and blessed at its end, not merely long.

basic.context: The book closes with God speaking again, this time to rebuke Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar directly, telling them they had not spoken accurately about God, as Job had, and that they must offer sacrifices and seek Job's own prayer on their behalf to avoid God's judgment. Once Job prays for these very friends, the LORD restores everything, doubling his flocks, giving him ten new children, and blessing him with a long, full life, ending with Job living to see four generations of descendants.
basic.hermeneutics: This ending must not be read as proof that suffering always ends in doubled material blessing, as though the book has secretly agreed with the friends' formula after all. The restoration comes specifically after Job's act of costly forgiveness, praying for the men who wounded him, and God's vindication centers on Job having 'spoken accurately' about Him, not on any formula of reward for good behavior.
basic.originalLanguages: God shuv, restores or turns back, Job's fortunes using language elsewhere applied to national restoration from exile, elevating this personal story to a picture of full reversal from ruin. Job's daughters receive a nachalah, inheritance, alongside their brothers, remarkable generosity in their ancient context. And Job dies saba, full and satisfied, with years, the same word used of Abraham's peaceful death.
basic.typology: Job's vindication after unjust suffering, and his role as the one whose intercession secures forgiveness for others, foreshadows Christ, the truly righteous sufferer whose intercession secures forgiveness for those who wronged Him, and whose resurrection is the pattern of restoration beyond suffering that Job's story only partially anticipates.
basic.christ: Job, having suffered unjustly, becomes the very one through whom his accusers find forgiveness, they cannot go to God directly but must come to Job first; this anticipates Jesus Christ, who suffered far more unjustly and now serves as our great High Priest and Intercessor, through whom alone sinners, even those who wronged Him, find reconciliation with God, 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 7:25.
basic.god: God is shown here as both the just Judge who rebukes false theology by name, and the gracious Restorer who blesses His faithful servant beyond his former state; God's justice and mercy operate together, first correcting, then abundantly restoring, without ever explaining to Job the reason for his original suffering.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Timothy 2:5 names Christ as the one Mediator through whom sinners approach God. Hebrews 7:25 says Christ always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. James 5:11 cites the Lord's compassion and mercy as displayed in how Job's story ends. Deuteronomy 30:3 uses the same 'restore the fortunes' language for God's future restoration of Israel.
basic.oneStory: Job's restoration follows his costly intercession for the friends who wronged him, a pattern the whole Bible carries forward to Jesus Christ, the truly innocent sufferer who intercedes for His enemies and secures a restoration, resurrection life, far greater than anything doubled wealth could picture.

context.literary:
The epilogue is in prose, and it is built as a mirror of the prologue. The book opened with a blameless man, his seven sons and three daughters, and his flocks counted in sevens and thousands, Job 1:1-3. It closes with the same man, the same family shape and the same flocks counted again, Job 42:12-13. In chapter 1 Job offers burnt offerings for his children, Job 1:5, and in 42:8 he is set to intercede again, this time for his friends. In chapter 1 the LORD calls Job 'My servant,' Job 1:8, and in 42:7-8 that title is spoken four times. In chapter 2 three friends come to sympathize with Job and comfort him, Job 2:11, and in 42:11 his family finish what the friends began.

Within the epilogue the movement is from words to action to blessing to death. First a speech from God to Eliphaz, 42:7-9. Then a change of fortune, 42:10-11, with the pivotal clause 'After Job had prayed for his friends.' Then the counted goods and the family, 42:12-15, and last a life summed up, 42:16-17. Four short scenes take the story from wrath to old age.

The details are chosen carefully. God addresses Eliphaz, the first of the friends to speak, and includes the other two in the verdict. The animals, in verse 12, are the exact doubles of Job 1:3, 7,000 sheep to 14,000, 3,000 camels to 6,000, 500 yoke of oxen to 1,000, 500 female donkeys to 1,000. The children are not doubled but restored to the same number, seven sons and three daughters, as if the first children are not simply replaced. And the daughters are named while the sons are not. In a book that has closely guarded God's silence about why, the ending is a lavish, warm scene rather than a verdict.

Elihu, who spoke at length in chapters 32 to 37, is absent from the closing account. He is neither rebuked nor commended.
context.historical:
The setting is the patriarchal world. Job acts as a family priest, sacrifices burnt offerings, and is wealthy in animals. There is no tabernacle, no Aaronic priesthood and no Sinai law. Seven bulls and seven rams are a full and costly offering in that world. Balaam asked for the same numbers before seeking a word from God for Balak, Numbers 23:1, and Hezekiah's priests later brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats as a sin offering, 2 Chronicles 29:21. Here the number marks completeness, not magic, and the offering is real.

The role of the wronged party as mediator is unusual and striking. In the ancient world a person who had sinned against another might seek reconciliation through a gift or a third party. God's command puts the injured man at the centre. The friends who had sat in judgment must come, contrite and with sacrifices, to the man they judged, and he must pray for them.

The gifts of 42:11 fit the customs of a close community. Each visitor gave a piece of silver and a gold ring. The BSB footnote notes that the value of the piece, the kesitah, is unknown today. It occurs in Genesis 33:19, where Jacob buys a plot of land. The ring might be worn in the nose or ear, as in Genesis 24:22 and Exodus 32:2, and it was portable wealth. The sum of small gifts helped a ruined man start again. It is also striking that the brothers and acquaintances who had turned away from Job, Job 19:13-14, come back and eat with him.

The gift of an inheritance to the daughters is unusual for its time. In Israel's later law daughters inherited only when there were no sons, Numbers 27:7-8. Job gives them a share 'among their brothers,' when they had brothers. His 140 years are within the range of the patriarchs, Abraham living 175, Genesis 25:7.
context.canonical:
Job's story is taken up in later Scripture as a settled fact of faith. Ezekiel lists Noah, Daniel and Job as men whose righteousness could deliver only themselves, Ezekiel 14:14 and 14:20. James holds Job up as an example of perseverance and appeals to what the Lord finally did: 'You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy,' James 5:11. The 'outcome' points to this epilogue, and James reads it as evidence of God's compassion, not as a reward system.

The picture of restoration draws on a set of biblical words. The idiom for restoring fortunes appears in the promises that God will bring the exiles home, Deuteronomy 30:3, Jeremiah 29:14 and Hosea 6:11, and in the prayer of Psalm 126:4. The image of a double portion appears in Isaiah 61:7, 'Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion,' and in Zechariah 9:12, 'I will restore to you double.' Job's ending is a small version of the return of Israel from exile.

The intercessor who prays for those who wronged him has a long line in Scripture. Abraham prays for Abimelech, Moses for Israel and for Miriam, Samuel for the people. In the New Testament Jesus tells His disciples to pray for those who persecute them, Matthew 5:44, Paul says to bless and not curse, Romans 12:14, and James says that the prayer of a righteous man has great power, James 5:16. Above all, Jesus prays 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, and Hebrews 7:25 says He always lives to intercede.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers to come away with three convictions. First, God's judgment of human theology is not the same as the judgment of human wisdom. The friends had spoken with confidence for nearly thirty chapters, and God tells them they were wrong, while the man they accused was right. A good many of the friends' sentences are true in isolation, as Eliphaz's picture of the old age of the righteous, Job 5:24-26, and Bildad's promise of flourishing latter days, Job 8:7, describe this very ending. The friends' error was to use those truths as a formula and to turn them against a suffering man.

Second, God is the one who restores, and He does so freely. The ending does not reveal a hidden bargain. Nothing in the text says Job's patience purchased his blessing, and the narrator says the blessing follows after he has prayed for his friends. It is a gift that looks like grace and is shaped by forgiveness.

Third, reconciliation in the community of God's people matters. The friends are not written off. There is a road back, and it runs through the person they hurt. The author wants readers to see that judgment and mercy work together, and that vindication does not exclude forgiveness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter records what God did for one man. It does not promise that every sufferer will be restored on earth with doubled goods. The New Testament makes the caution plain. Hebrews 11:36-39 speaks of faithful people who were flogged, imprisoned and killed, and who 'did not receive what was promised.' To read the epilogue as a promise of prosperity is to bring back the friends' formula through the back door.

It also does not say that the new children erased the old ones. Job's grief is not addressed in the text, and it would be unkind to take the ending as saying that pain is cured by replacement. What the ending honours is that God's blessing follows the suffering, and that it is real.

What does carry forward is the command implied in the story: to pray for those who have wronged us, as Jesus later teaches, Matthew 5:44. The passage also encourages confidence that God's purposes for a sufferer are compassionate, as James says, James 5:11, even when the outcome is not visible until the end. The offerings are not repeated, since Christ's sacrifice has completed them, Hebrews 9:14, but the pattern of coming to God through a mediator remains.

debates.question: What does it mean that Job spoke 'accurately' about God?

views.label: Job's laments and protests were honest and true to God
views.case: Job refused to invent sins to fit the friends' formula, and he brought his anguish to God, not about God to others. The Hebrew of 42:7 can be read 'to Me,' and if so, the contrast is that Job spoke to God while the friends spoke about Him, Job 13:7-8. God prefers honest lament to false defence.

views.label: Job was right in his main claim, not in every word
views.case: Job was right that suffering is not always punishment, and right that he had not committed the sins alleged. He was wrong at times about God's justice, and God told him so in 38 to 41. The verdict of 42:7 is about the central question of the book.

views.label: Job is right because he repented
views.case: Some read 42:7 in the light of 42:1-6: Job now speaks rightly because he has seen God. The verdict then covers his final words more than the whole dialogue.

debates.bearing: The first and second are best supported by the flow of the book. Job's honesty and his refusal of the formula are praised, and his repentance in chapter 42 shows he was not beyond correction. Both are true of him.

debates.question: Does the ending restore the retribution formula after all?

views.label: Yes, the good are finally rewarded
views.case: Job ends with more than he began, and Bildad had promised, 'Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish,' Job 8:7. The friends' theology looks vindicated in outcome, and some readers feel the book has come back to the old scheme.

views.label: No, the ending is grace, not payment
views.case: God's rebuke of the friends shows their scheme was wrong. Job is restored after he has prayed for them, not because his suffering was earned back. James reads the ending as displaying the Lord's compassion, not His accounting, James 5:11. And the reader knows from chapters 1 and 2 that the suffering did not come as punishment.

debates.bearing: The second reading is the book's own. The friends were right that God sometimes blesses the righteous, and wrong about why Job suffered and how God works. The ending is the freedom of a generous God, not the operation of a machine.

debates.question: Why is Elihu missing from the ending?

views.label: Elihu was substantially right
views.case: His speeches prepare the way for the storm, since the thunder he describes in Job 37 rolls into the whirlwind of 38:1. He is not among those God rebukes, so he needs no correction.

views.label: Elihu is left out because he does not matter to the outcome
views.case: The three friends had been addressed as those who came to comfort Job. Elihu appears without introduction and disappears without comment, and some scholars believe his speeches were added later. The epilogue simply never mentions him.

debates.bearing: The text does not say. What is clear is that God's verdict is directed at those who insisted on a formula, and that Elihu, who spoke of God's greatness and of a mediator, is not counted among them.

study.originalLanguages:
God's verdict in 42:7 turns on the word nekonah, translated 'accurately' in the BSB. It comes from the root kun, 'to be firm, to be established,' the same root as the 'steadfast' spirit of Psalm 51:10. To speak nekonah is to speak what stands, what is true and stable. The Hebrew literally says 'you have not spoken to Me nekonah,' with a preposition that most naturally means 'to,' though many versions render 'about.' If 'to' is the sense, the contrast is between Job, who addressed God, and the friends, who talked about Him in the third person.

The title 'My servant' is ebed, and it is used four times in 42:7-8. It is the title God gives to those He trusts and uses, such as Moses, of whom He says, 'this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house,' Numbers 12:7. It was given to Job at the beginning, Job 1:8, and it is given again, undiminished, after all that Job has said in anguish.

The word 'folly' in 42:8 is nevalah. It belongs to the family of nabal, the fool. In 1 Samuel 25:25 Abigail says of her husband, 'His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.' In Hebrew thought, the fool is not stupid but morally dull, one who acts as though God will not notice. The friends' folly was to speak for God without regard for Him.

God says He will 'accept' Job's prayer, and the idiom is nasa panim, literally 'lift the face.' Verse 8 says, 'I will lift his face,' and verse 9 says that the LORD lifted Job's face. It is the language of favour, a superior lifting up the countenance of one who bows, and it also means to receive someone graciously. Here it is repeated to underline that God's response to Job's prayer for the friends is personal and warm.

The phrase 'restored his prosperity' is shav et-shevut, the idiom that recurs in the promise of Israel's return, Deuteronomy 30:3 and Psalm 126:4. Its noun, shevut, is usually rendered 'captivity' or 'fortunes,' and the meaning is a reversal of the bondage of loss. The verb for 'doubled' is built on mishneh, a double, the word of Isaiah 61:7 and Zechariah 9:12.

Finally, 42:11 says that the visitors 'consoled' and 'comforted' Job. These are the words of 2:11, where the friends came 'to sympathize with Job and comfort him.' The verbs return, and this time they are carried out. The word for 'adversity' is ra'ah, the word Job used in 2:10 when he asked whether we should accept adversity from God. The narrator lets the family say what Job said, that the LORD brought it, and does not correct them.

typology.type: Job as the wronged man who intercedes, Job 42:8-10
typology.fulfillment: Job prays for the men who accused him, and God accepts his prayer. This is the pattern the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ, who prays from the cross, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34. Isaiah's Servant 'made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, and Hebrews says Christ always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25. The correspondence is that the wounded one becomes the way of reconciliation. It escalates in that Job was himself a sinner interceding in his own household, while Christ is the sinless mediator who bears the sins He prays about.

typology.type: Burnt offerings for those under wrath, Job 42:8
typology.fulfillment: The friends must bring seven bulls and seven rams, and the offering covers them from the wrath the LORD has spoken. The Old Testament sacrifices taught that sin requires a death and that God provides a way. Christ 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2, and offered Himself unblemished to purify our consciences, Hebrews 9:14. Where the friends brought costly animals through a priest, believers come through a Priest who is also the offering. The type falls short because the bulls and rams could only picture what Christ's sacrifice actually accomplished.

The LORD restores Job's fortunes and blesses his latter days more than his first. The New Testament turns this into hope beyond this life. Peter writes that after we have suffered a little while, the God of all grace will Himself restore, secure, strengthen and establish us, 1 Peter 5:10. Paul sets present sufferings against a glory not comparable to them, Romans 8:18, and Christ's own resurrection is the firstfruits of a restoration that includes the body, 1 Corinthians 15:20. Job received his restoration within his earthly lifetime and then died; the resurrection promises a restoration that death cannot undo, Revelation 21:4.

typology.type: Daughters who inherit among their brothers, Job 42:15
typology.fulfillment: The generosity of the inheritance given to Job's daughters anticipates the inclusive inheritance of the gospel. In Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female,' and all who belong to Him are 'heirs according to the promise,' Galatians 3:28-29. Paul writes that children of God are 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17. The correspondence is one of pattern only, since Job's practice is not presented as a prophecy. It falls short because Job's daughters received a share of goods, while believers receive a share in Christ Himself.

study.christ:
The epilogue leads to Christ first by the figure of the servant. God calls Job 'My servant' four times in two verses, and it is the title of the one who is faithful and trusted. In Isaiah the title becomes the name of the promised Servant: 'Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' Isaiah 52:13, and Matthew applies the servant songs to Jesus, 'Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen,' Matthew 12:18. Isaiah 53:10 describes the Servant in language that echoes Job's ending, for after suffering 'He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days.' The Servant's story is like Job's, but with an unimaginably heavier weight: He suffers not merely without cause but for the sake of others, and He is vindicated by resurrection, Romans 1:4, and 'vindicated by the Spirit,' 1 Timothy 3:16.

It leads to Christ by intercession. Job's prayer for his friends is the hinge on which the whole ending turns, and it is a prayer for those who had hurt him. Jesus prays for those who nailed Him up, Luke 23:34. Peter tells the crowd who had put Him to death that they acted in ignorance, that God had foretold His Christ would suffer, and calls them to repent, Acts 3:17-19. The parallel is exact in shape: the friends must come to the very person they wronged, and the wronged one prays for them. In Christ, those who wounded Him find that the way back to God runs through Him. Hebrews 7:25 says that He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them, and 1 John 2:1 calls Him an advocate before the Father.

It leads to Christ by the failure of the friends' scheme. The friends said that suffering follows sin, and Job cried out for a mediator, Job 9:33. In Christ the truth is different from both. The one who suffered most had no sin, and His suffering is the price of forgiveness for others. The priestly offerings of Job 42:8 are replaced by the one offering of Christ, who gave Himself up as a fragrant sacrifice, Ephesians 5:2.

It leads to Christ by vindication beyond the grave. Job is restored within his years and dies old. Jesus is raised and does not die again, and His people are promised the same. Paul says Christ is the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

A caution. Job is not a prediction of Jesus, and the book never says so. The New Testament draws on the pattern of the righteous sufferer who intercedes and is vindicated, and finds that the pattern reaches its fullness in Christ. That is the honest limit of the link.
study.god:
The epilogue shows a God who cares what is said about Him. 'My wrath is kindled against you,' He says to Eliphaz, 'for you have not spoken about Me accurately,' 42:7. God does not need defenders who lie. Job had already warned them, 'Will you speak wickedly on God's behalf or speak deceitfully for Him?' Job 13:7. A God who is offended by false comfort is a God who takes suffering seriously. It also tells the church something about the ethics of theology: we may not say what we do not know in God's name.

He is a God who is also merciful to those whose folly He rebukes. He does not destroy the friends. He offers them a costly, gracious road back, and sets the one they wronged in the middle of it. The condition of their acceptance is humility, since they must go to Job. This is the shape of the gospel in embryo.

He honours the sufferer. He calls Job 'My servant' after Job has cried out, doubted and repented. There is no hint that Job's complaints have cancelled his standing. God confirms that the man He allowed to be tested had spoken more truly of Him than the men who defended Him.

He vindicates His own confidence in Job. In chapter 1, Satan asked, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' Job 1:9. The ending is the answer. Job served God when God did nothing for him but be present, and he kept faith when the reason for pain was withheld. God's claim that such a person exists is borne out. This is the deepest thing the ending says about God: He is worth loving for Himself.

He is free to bless. The blessing is not a wage. It arrives after intercession and with no explanation, and it is out of proportion to any earning, 'more than his first,' 42:12. The God of the epilogue is the God James calls full of compassion and mercy, James 5:11.

He holds sovereignty over adversity without explaining it. The family says the LORD 'brought' the adversity, 42:11, and the narrator lets it stand. The book has shown that the adversary acted within limits God set, Job 1:12 and 2:6, and the ending does not resolve the mystery of how those two facts fit. It asks the reader to hold both, as Job did in 2:10.

For worship, the passage teaches gratitude that does not need to be explained, and it shows that God's dealings with the wounded end in compassion. The grief is real, the mystery remains, and the last word is generosity.

crossReferences.note: Satan's challenge, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?', is the question the whole book has been answering. The ending vindicates God's confidence in Job, and shows that a person can hold on to God when he is stripped of every gain. The epilogue is the reply to this accusation.
Job's three friends came to sympathize with him and comfort him. In 42:11 the same two verbs return for his family, this time carried out. The book completes what the friends began and did badly.

Job warned the friends that they were speaking wickedly and deceitfully on God's behalf. God's verdict in 42:7 confirms the warning. It shows that a defence of God that is not true is no service to Him.

Eliphaz had said that God would deliver even the guilty through the cleanness of a righteous man's hands. He meant it against Job, but in 42:8 it comes true of Eliphaz himself: Job's prayer delivers him. The irony is one of the book's finest.

Bildad promised that if Job were pure and upright, his latter days would flourish. Job's ending looks like the promise, but the book has shown that the promise was used as an accusation. The event agrees with the friends, and the reasoning does not.

God speaks of Moses as 'My servant' who is faithful in all His house and to whom He speaks face to face. Job is given the same title, four times in two verses. It puts a man outside Israel on the level of Israel's greatest prophet in God's regard.

Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as men of proverbial righteousness, whose righteousness could deliver only themselves. Job's standing as one of the righteous in Israel's memory is the background to God's verdict in 42:7.

The psalm prays for restoration like streams in the Negev and promises that those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy. It uses the same restoring idiom as Job 42:10, and it sets Job's story within Israel's hope that weeping is not the end.

Instead of shame, God's people will have a double portion. Job's doubled goods are a small picture of this promise, in which shame is answered by honour. The prophet applies it to a whole nation returning from exile, and Job's private ending shows the same generosity at the scale of one household.

James tells suffering believers to remember Job's perseverance and the outcome from the Lord, who is full of compassion and mercy. The apostle reads the epilogue as a demonstration of God's character, not as a formula for how to be rewarded.

From the cross Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them.' The wronged one intercedes for those who wronged Him, as Job did for the friends. In Christ the pattern reaches its fullness, for He is both the wounded and the way of reconciliation.

Christ is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them. This is the settled version of what Job did once. The friends came through Job; believers come through a Priest who never dies.

After a little suffering, the God of all grace will Himself restore, secure, strengthen and establish His people. Peter promises the substance of Job's ending, and places it in the hands of God, whose timing may be beyond this life.

study.oneStory:
The book of Job opens in a world where the adversary can strike, and it ends with the adversary out of sight and a man with a full table. That movement summarises the shape of the Bible. Genesis 3 brought a curse on the ground and death into the world. From that point, all human beings suffer, and the righteous suffer with the rest. The story of Scripture is God's answer to the fact of suffering, and Job's epilogue is a small preview of the answer.

The epilogue picks up promises made earlier in the story. The God who set Israel free promised to restore fortunes after judgment, Deuteronomy 30:3, and the prophets spoke of double portions and of return, Isaiah 61:7 and Zechariah 9:12. Job's blessing is a sample of that restoration within a single life. The text also fills out Israel's understanding of how God deals with suffering: not every trouble is punishment, and God's servants may be vindicated without their suffering being explained.

The New Testament brings the pattern to its centre in Christ. He is the righteous sufferer who needed no repentance and who prays for those who hurt Him. His resurrection is the vindication of the Servant, Romans 1:4, and the restoration that Job received in part is given in fullness. The many who once wronged Him are called to repent and turn back, Acts 3:19. Hebrews 11:36-39 reminds us that many faithful people died without receiving what was promised, and so the epilogue points beyond itself: the final restoration is not to be found in earthly doubled flocks.

That final restoration is the new creation. Romans 8:18-22 speaks of the creation waiting to be set free. Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that there will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain. Job's family sat and ate with him in his house; the redeemed will eat at a table in the presence of God. The sufferer is not only restored to what he had; he is brought into what he was made for.

In the meantime the church lives as Job's friends did after the verdict: reconciled through the intercession of the One they wronged, and called to pray for others in the same way. It lives in the hope of James 5:11, that the outcome from the Lord is compassion and mercy, even when the way there is hard.

sermon.title: Job: Reversal in Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon is preached directly on Job 42:7-17, tracing how God humbles the three friends and requires Job's intercession for them, and how Job's willingness to forgive and pray for his accusers proves the genuineness of his own repentance before God restores his fortunes.

quiz.q: What does God say to Eliphaz in 42:7?

options.text: That His wrath is kindled against Eliphaz and his two friends because they had not spoken about God accurately, as Job had.
options.note: This is God's direct, explicit verdict vindicating Job's speech over the friends' theology.

options.text: That Job had spoken wrongly and needed to apologize to the friends.
options.note: The verdict is the reverse; God rebukes the friends, not Job, for wrong speech.

options.text: That all four men, including Job, had spoken equally wrongly.
options.note: God singles out the three friends specifically; Job is commended, not condemned, in this verse.

options.text: That the friends should offer sacrifices as general worship, apart from any specific connection to Job's own prayer.
options.note: Close, sacrifices are indeed required, but verses 8-9 specifically tie their effectiveness to Job's own intercessory prayer, not sacrifice alone.

quiz.q: What must the three friends do to avoid God dealing with them according to their folly?

options.text: Offer a burnt offering and have Job pray for them, since God will accept Job's prayer on their behalf.
options.note: Verses 8-9 describe exactly this process, and the friends carry it out.

options.text: Simply apologize directly to God with no further action.
options.note: God specifically requires the sacrifice and Job's intercessory prayer, not merely private apology.

options.text: Give all their wealth to Job.
options.note: The text specifies sacrificial animals and Job's prayer, not a transfer of wealth.

options.text: Publicly confess their theological error before the whole community, apart from any specific ritual action.
options.note: Close in spirit, real humility before Job is required, but God specifically commands the concrete acts of sacrifice and Job's prayer, not merely public confession.

quiz.q: When does the LORD restore Job's fortunes, according to 42:10?

options.text: After Job had prayed for his friends.
options.note: The verse explicitly ties the timing of restoration to Job's act of intercession for the very men who had wronged him.

options.text: Immediately after God's first speech to Job in chapter 38.
options.note: The restoration comes only after this later act of Job's prayer for his friends, in chapter 42.

options.text: Before Job's repentance in 42:1-6.
options.note: Job's repentance and confession, and then his intercession for his friends, both precede the restoration.

options.text: Sometime after God's whirlwind speeches, though the text does not specify the precise trigger.
options.note: Close on the general timing, but 42:10 is specific and explicit: restoration follows directly from Job's prayer for his friends.

quiz.q: What is notable about how Job treats his three daughters in 42:13-15?

options.text: He grants them an inheritance alongside their seven brothers, an act of generosity beyond typical ancient custom.
options.note: In the ancient world, daughters typically inherited only in the absence of sons, making Job's provision for his daughters notably generous.

options.text: He excludes them entirely from any inheritance.
options.note: Verse 15 explicitly states he granted them an inheritance among their brothers.

options.text: He gives all his wealth only to his daughters.
options.note: The inheritance is shared between sons and daughters, not given exclusively to the daughters.

options.text: He names his daughters individually but leaves his seven sons unnamed in the text.
options.note: Close, the text does specifically name only the daughters, which actually strengthens the point that Job gives his daughters distinctive honor alongside their inheritance.

quiz.q: How does Job's role in interceding for his friends anticipate Christ?

options.text: It foreshadows Christ's ongoing intercession for those who come to God through Him, even praying for those who wronged Him.
options.note: Hebrews 7:25 and Luke 23:34 both show Christ interceding for and forgiving those who had wronged Him, the pattern Job models here.

options.text: It teaches that intercession for others is unnecessary and unhelpful.
options.note: The passage presents Job's intercession as effective and necessary for his friends' reconciliation with God.

options.text: It shows that only priests, never ordinary believers, can intercede for others.
options.note: Job is not a priest in this narrative; his role as intercessor points forward to the priesthood of all believers made possible through Christ.

options.text: It connects generally to biblical teaching on forgiveness, without a specific New Testament parallel to Job's intercessory role.
options.note: Close in a general sense, but Hebrews 7:25 and Luke 23:34 provide remarkably specific parallels to Job's particular act of praying for those who wronged him.

questions: God vindicates Job's honest speech over the friends' confident theology. Where might you need to trust that honest lament before God matters more to Him than having all the right answers?

Job's restoration comes only after he prays for the very friends who wounded him. Is there someone who has hurt you that God may be calling you to forgive and intercede for, even before you feel fully ready?

Job's daughters receive an inheritance beyond what custom required. Where do you see God's restoration in your own life going beyond simply replacing what was lost, into genuinely new and generous blessing?
The book ends without ever explaining to Job the reason his suffering began. How do you make peace with unresolved questions in your own life while still trusting God's goodness?
Job's intercession for his friends anticipates Christ's ongoing prayer for us. How does knowing Jesus intercedes for you even now change how you approach God in your weakest, most guilty moments?

translationNotes.note: 'You have not spoken about Me accurately' is repeated twice, in verses 7 and 8, for emphasis, underscoring that the friends' theological error, not merely their harshness, is the specific charge against them.

'A piece of silver' translates kesitah, a rare and otherwise obscure unit of currency mentioned elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Joshua 24:32, suggesting an archaic or foreign monetary term appropriate to the patriarchal setting of Job's story.

'Saw his children and their children to the fourth generation' is itself a traditional biblical picture of a full, blessed life, paralleling the patriarchal narratives and underscoring that Job's restoration extended across his whole remaining lifetime, not merely a single reversal of fortune.
